lines: The one by the kitchen door, where everything unclassifiable goes to wait: a stamp, a key to nothing, three dead batteries, a recipe for a cake nobody remembers eating, a button that was clearly important to someone, once.
I have started to think of the drawer as a diary written by objects.

When my father died I opened his, and found forty years of small decisions: spare fuses (he was a cautious man), a photograph of a goat (he was not), and a note in his handwriting that said only: Ask Dami about the tap.
I still do not know what the tap was, or what I was meant to say.
But I read that note aloud, in the empty kitchen, and the house seemed to lean in to listen.
We are all, in the end, a drawer.
A little untidy, mostly harmless, holding on to things in case they turn out to be necessary.
The tap, I have decided, was him, still keeping an eye on the house.
